analysis.one_liner: Bars officeholders from taking payments from foreign governments and bars the President from taking payments from any government besides his salary.
analysis.headline: Introduced in November 2021 with 10 cosponsors and referred to the Senate Homeland Security Committee, which never held a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write the Constitution's emoluments rules into federal law. It would make it illegal for any federal officeholder, including the President and Vice President, to accept anything of value from a foreign government without Congress's consent, and illegal for the President to accept anything of value from the federal or a state government beyond his official salary. It would give the Office of Government Ethics power to fine violators and force them to disgorge the money, let the House or Senate sue violators in federal court, require the Office of Special Counsel to investigate complaints within 120 days, and add new disclosure requirements for gifts and payments from foreign governments.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, in the form of a government whose decisions cannot be bought with payments to officeholders. The bill's stated purpose is that elected leaders stay dependent on the people alone rather than on anyone offering private financial rewards. It also protects federal workers with diversified investments by exempting small, remote holdings from the ban.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyday citizens relying on an unbought government

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for any federal officeholder, including the President and Vice President, to accept a present, payment, office, or title from a foreign government without Congress's consent first [S2][S3].
Prohibits the President from accepting anything of value from the federal government or a state beyond his legally set salary, so state and federal officials cannot buy influence with him [S2][S3].

Defines emolument broadly to include any profit, gain, or advantage, even payments from ordinary commercial transactions regardless of whether they are at fair market value, and applies the ban to businesses or trusts the officeholder owns an interest in [S3].

Gives the Office of Government Ethics authority to issue fines, order divestiture or disgorgement, and sue violators, and requires the Office of Special Counsel to complete investigations within 120 days and report to Congress [S2][S3].

Lets the House or Senate itself sue a violator in a fast-tracked three-judge court, with remedies including disgorgement of the value of foreign payments and surrender of prohibited foreign titles [S3].

Adds annual public disclosure of any present or payment received from a foreign government, including the source, date, and value, plus disclosure of financial arrangements expected to produce foreign payments [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Presidents, vice presidents, and other officeholders who own businesses that receive money from foreign or domestic governments would lose that revenue and face fines, disgorgement, and lawsuits. Foreign governments lose a channel for currying favor with U.S. officials.

drawbacks.text: The bill lets one branch of government, Congress, sue the sitting President directly, which creates a standing interbranch legal fight and could invite politically motivated suits by whichever party controls a chamber [S3].

The definition of emolument sweeps in payments from ordinary commercial transactions even at fair market value, which business-linked officeholders and some scholars argue is broader than the Constitution's original meaning and hard to apply in practice [S3].

Handing an independent ethics office power to fine a President raises separation-of-powers questions an honest supporter would acknowledge, since critics contend the executive branch cannot easily police its own head [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and hard to dispute: a president's or officeholder's business would no longer be able to collect payments from foreign or state governments with no legal consequence and no disclosure. The costs are legal and procedural rather than pocketbook: enforcement could trigger constitutional fights over Congress suing the President, and the broad definition could catch ordinary commercial dealings. The bill tries to manage this with exemptions for diversified holdings and small-value gifts, and with a severability clause, though those carve-outs also open room for gamesmanship.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Blumenthal introduced the bill on November 4, 2021 with nine Democratic cosponsors listed on the introduced version [S1][S3].
Ten senators in total, nine Democrats and one Independent, cosponsored the bill; no Republican did [S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs on the day of introduction, and no further action was ever recorded [S5].
The committee never held a hearing or markup, and the full Senate never voted on the bill before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Officeholders with private business interests, above all whoever occupied the presidency, kept the existing arrangement in which payments from foreign and domestic governments carry no statutory penalty and no special disclosure requirement. Ethics enforcement remains limited to the constitutional clauses' unclear and untested remedies.

for.name: Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate on November 4, 2021.

for.name: 10 senators (9 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Whitehouse, Markey, Warren, Hirono, Booker, Sanders, Wyden, Gillibrand, Klobuchar, and one Independent.

against.name: Gary Peters
against.role: Chair, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred to his committee; no committee action appears in the record before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors were Democrats or the Senate's Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill also never moved in the Democratic-run committee.

industries.industry: Officeholders' private businesses (hospitality, real estate, and licensing ventures tied to elected officials)
industries.note: These businesses profit from payments and patronage from foreign and state governments; the bill would ban most of that revenue, force disgorgement of past gains, and require public disclosure of the payments. Their gain is the public's cost, since the payments are exactly what the bill targets as a route of influence over officials.

industries.industry: Ethics enforcement infrastructure (Office of Government Ethics, Office of Special Counsel)
industries.note: The bill would hand both offices new legal powers: fines, divestiture orders, and civil suits for OGE, and mandatory 120-day investigations for the Special Counsel. Their institutional interest in having an enforceable mandate runs alongside the public's interest in accountability.
